test.query: What constraints to broader application of anti-PD-1 therapies does this paper mention?
test.identifier_note: The live call used the current DOI/title paper reference. No identifier contract was changed.

actual_mcp_result.brief_summary: The paper states that broader use of systemic anti-PD-1/PD-L1 monoclonal antibodies is constrained by large molecular size, limited tumor penetration, long systemic exposure, immune-related toxicities, high production costs, and variable patient responses. It presents anti-PD-1 scFvs as smaller, modular alternatives that may improve local delivery and reduce systemic exposure, while noting that scFv platforms still face translation barriers.
key_findings: Full-length anti-PD-1/PD-L1 antibodies are described as large molecules that do not readily penetrate tumors.
Long antibody half-lives are linked to immune-related adverse events such as colitis and pneumonitis.
High production costs and interpatient heterogeneity in response are cited as barriers to widespread use.
Fc-mediated effector functions may contribute to off-tumor toxicities in some non-responders.

Anti-PD-1 scFv approaches face their own constraints, including short serum half-life, aggregation risk, immunogenicity, manufacturing scalability, vector standardization, antiviral immunity, and dose-limiting toxicity assessment in early trials.
actual_mcp_result.method_overview: This is a review article summarizing anti-PD-1 scFv discovery, engineering, delivery platforms, cell-based therapies, viral/gene-delivery systems, and early clinical translation. No primary experimental protocol is provided in the supplied context.

source_lines.content: The programmed death-1 (PD-1) immune checkpoint is a core regulator of T-cell exhaustion and immune evasion in cancer. While PD-1/PD-L1 monoclonal antibodies have changed the landscape of cancer immunotherapy, there are barriers to broader application due to their large size, potential for systemic toxicities, and high production costs. In this review article, we will focus on therapeutic development, functional applications, and translational advances of anti-PD-1 singlechain variable fragments (scFvs). Advances in phage-display libraries, immunization methods, and antibody engineering have helped develop high-affinity scFvs with novel structural and mechanistic properties. Direct functional applications incorporating anti-PD-1 scFvs are bispecific and trispecific constructs, antibody–drug conjugates (ADCs), immunotoxins, nanoparticles, and biological vector carriers that incorporate checkpoint blockade with targeted cytotoxicity or immunostimulation. Engineered immune cells, such as armored CAR-Ts, NK cells, and MSCs, can secrete or display anti-PD-1 scFvs within the tumor to provide localized checkpoint inhibition, enhance effector-cell persistence, and remodel the tumor microenvironment. Oncolytic and non-replicating viral vectors can further confine scFv activity to tumors, coupling checkpoint blockade with oncolysis, cytokine expression, or bispecific T-cell engagers. Early-phase clinical trials are currently studying TILs and CAR-TILs engineered to secrete scFvs and oncolytic HSV-1 encoding multifunctional checkpoint payloads across a variety of solid tumors. Taken together, anti-PD-1 scFvs represent a modular platform for localized checkpoint inhibition and potentially improved cost-effectiveness compared with systemic antibodies. Future work should prioritize rational combination strategies and well-designed clinical trials that integrate anti-PD-1 scFv platforms with other immunotherapies and standard treatments to maximize clinical benefit.

loaded_context_blocks.relevance_reason: The introduction expands the barriers into tumor penetration, adverse events, cost, response heterogeneity, off-tumor toxicity, and scFv-specific limitations.

source_lines.content: Escaping this checkpoint with blocking antibodies, such as nivolumab or pembrolizumab, prevents ligand binding and restores proximal TCR signaling and effector cytokine production. Although these systemic antibody therapies have shown long-term durable responses in patients with melanoma, lung cancer, and renal carcinoma, significant challenges remain [10–12]. Antibodies are large (∼150 kDa) and do not readily penetrate tumors; they have long half-lives, which contribute to immunotherapeutic related adverse events, including colitis and pneumonitis, in the clinical setting, as well as production costs and interpatient heterogeneity in response, limiting more widespread use [13–16]. In addition, Fc-mediated antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC) and other effector functions can contribute to off-tumor toxicities in non-responders, as suggested by preclinical and clinical correlative studies reporting increased immune-related adverse events despite limited antitumor benefit [17].

Single-chain variable fragments (scFvs) offer an appealing alternative format. scFvs are generated by joining the VH and VL domains of an antibody with a flexible linker. The resulting protein is approximately 27–30 kDa and retains antigen specificity without the Fc domain. This low molecular weight facilitates greater tissue diffusion throughout the body and improved penetration into three-dimensional tumor spheroids compared with full-length antibodies in preclinical models [18, 19]. scFvs are suitable for microbial expression systems and are easily genetically incorporated into various delivery platforms, including chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells, oncolytic viruses, and nanoparticles [20]. Furthermore, scFvs circumvent off-target immune activation associated with Fc-mediated effector functions, allowing for the modular engineering of bispecific, trispecific, or fusion constructs. Most importantly, scFvs can be secreted or displayed locally within tumors, allowing checkpoint blockade to be focused where it is needed while disregarding peripheral tissues. Nevertheless, scFvs also have limitations, including short serum half-life, a propensity for aggregation, and potential immunogenicity, which necessitate careful engineering and formulation strategies to optimize clinical translation [21, 22].
